Brian McLaren
BRY-uhn muh-KLAIR-uhn
n. (a proper name; a contemporary emergent author)
Brian D. McLaren (b. 1956), American author and a founding voice of the Emergent Church, author of A New Kind of Christianity (2010). The surname is of Scottish Gaelic origin, “son of Lawrence.”

Biblical Definition

Brian McLaren is an American author and a leading voice of the so-called emergent or progressive movement, whose writings, including A Generous Orthodoxy and A New Kind of Christianity, have promoted a fundamental reimagining of the Christian faith. Under the banner of conversation and humility, the emergent framework recasts the historic gospel: the authority and inerrancy of Scripture are softened into a flexible narrative; the substitutionary atonement of Christ is questioned and even derided; the wrath of God and eternal conscious punishment are recast as unworthy of a loving God; the exclusivity of Christ as the only Savior is blurred toward a hopeful universalism; and the moral teaching of Scripture, especially on sexuality, is revised to suit the spirit of the age. This is not a fresh expression of the faith once delivered but a corruption of it, a different gospel which is not another (Galatians 1:7). Where the apostle thunders that a man is justified by faith in Christ apart from works, the emergent project dissolves the very categories of guilt, propitiation, and saving faith into a vague program of social betterment and an open-ended spiritual journey. The Church must answer such teaching not with hostility of spirit but with the clarity of Scripture: there is one gospel, one Mediator, one atonement, and one name under heaven by which we must be saved. McLaren’s influence is a summons to vigilance, for the most dangerous error wears the borrowed clothing of Christianity while emptying it of its saving content.

Webster 1828 Definition

Brian McLaren, a founding voice of the emergent/progressive movement whose A New Kind of Christianity reimagines and corrupts the historic gospel.

BRIAN MCLAREN, n. Brian D. McLaren (b. 1956), American author and emergent-church leader; surname of Scottish Gaelic origin, son of Lawrence.

A chief promoter of the emergent or “progressive” reframing of Christianity, author of A New Kind of Christianity.

A teacher who questions biblical authority, substitutionary atonement, hell, and the exclusivity of Christ.

A figure whose project the Church must name as a corruption of the gospel and rebut on biblical grounds.

Against such teaching stands the apostle: “Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).

Key Scripture

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

John 14:6 — "Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me."

Acts 4:12 — "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."

2 Tim 4:3 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;"

Modern Corruption

The emergent/progressive framework McLaren champions is itself a corruption of the gospel, hollowing out Scripture, atonement, and the exclusivity of Christ.

expand to see more

The corruption is the emergent or “progressive” reimagining of Christianity itself, advanced under the appealing language of conversation, humility, and a “journey of faith.” In McLaren’s framework the inerrancy of Scripture is loosened, penal substitution is mocked as “cosmic child abuse,” the wrath of God and eternal hell are recast as embarrassments, and the exclusive claim of Christ in John 14:6 is dissolved toward universalism. Strip these away and nothing of the saving gospel remains; what is left is moralism and sentiment dressed in Christian vocabulary. The proper rebuttal is not contempt but clarity: Scripture is breathed out by God and inerrant, Christ truly bore our penalty, hell is real and eternal, and there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12).

Underlying the project is the postmodern denial of fixed truth, which treats every doctrine as a provisional story to be renegotiated. But Paul warned of a day when men would not endure sound doctrine but heap up teachers to suit their own desires (2 Timothy 4:3), and he pronounced anathema on any other gospel, even from an angel (Galatians 1:8). To recover here is to hold fast the faith once for all delivered to the saints, contending for it with the gentleness commanded yet without surrendering one article of the truth.

Hebrew Roots

McLaren’s teaching roots in the postmodern emergent movement’s revision of historic Christianity.
